title: FDA v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp.
lead: The Food and Drug Administration tried to reduce youth tobacco use by treating nicotine as a drug and tobacco products as delivery devices. The Supreme Court concluded that Congress’s existing tobacco legislation excluded that authority under the statutory scheme then in force.

actors.name: Food and Drug Administration
actors.role: Federal regulator that adopted the tobacco rules

actors.name: Brown & Williamson and other respondents
actors.role: Manufacturers, retailers, and advertisers challenging the rules

proceedings: District court upheld jurisdiction and some rules; Fourth Circuit reversed for lack of jurisdiction; Supreme Court affirmed, 5–4.
limits: This account concerns the historical statutory framework before the Court in 2000, not present FDA tobacco authority. It transforms the supplied full brief and does not provide a new opinion audit or current citator assessment.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An agency revisits its tobacco position
paragraphs: The Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act authorized the Food and Drug Administration, or FDA, to regulate drugs and devices, including nonfood articles intended to affect bodily structure or function. The Act also addressed combination products. For many years, the FDA disclaimed authority over tobacco products sold without therapeutic claims. Meanwhile, Congress enacted six tobacco-and-health laws beginning in 1965, regulating warnings, advertising, research, and incentives for state restrictions on sales to minors.

In 1995, the FDA proposed a new approach. The agency concluded that nicotine was a drug and that cigarettes and smokeless tobacco were nicotine-delivery devices. Nicotine produced addiction, stimulation, tranquilization, and weight-control effects. The FDA found manufacturer intent from foreseeable effects, consumers’ reasons for use, and industry research and product design showing deliberate delivery of active doses. Its historical record attributed more than 400,000 deaths annually to tobacco and found that most adult smokers had begun before age eighteen.

sections.title: The FDA regulates access and promotion
paragraphs: The FDA issued a final rule aimed at preventing initiation among children and adolescents. It prohibited sales to people under eighteen, required photographic identification for purchasers under twenty-seven, restricted package sizes, samples, and self-service sales, and confined vending machines to adult-only locations. Advertising formats and locations, branded promotional items, and sponsorships also faced restrictions; products had to bear a nicotine-delivery-device label.

The agency used the Act’s restricted-device provision, § 360j(e), claiming that access and promotion controls could reasonably assure safety. It considered an outright ban more harmful because addicted consumers might suffer withdrawal, treatment resources might be strained, and illicit products might be more dangerous.

sections.title: The challenge moves through two lower courts
paragraphs: Tobacco manufacturers, retailers, and advertisers, including Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corporation, challenged the rules in the Middle District of North Carolina. They contested the FDA’s jurisdiction, its device-rule authority, and the rules’ constitutionality under the First Amendment.

The district court upheld jurisdiction and the access and labeling provisions but held that § 360j(e) did not authorize the advertising and promotion restrictions. It stayed the upheld provisions except the prohibition on sales to minors and certified an interlocutory appeal. The Fourth Circuit reversed because the FDA lacked tobacco jurisdiction. That conclusion made it unnecessary to decide the alternative statutory-power and constitutional issues. The Supreme Court agreed to review authority over tobacco as customarily marketed, without therapeutic claims.

sections.title: The majority reads the definitions in their statutory setting
paragraphs: Justice O’Connor’s five-Justice majority applied Chevron, the then-governing framework asking first whether Congress had answered the precise statutory question. Although respondents argued that manufacturer intent required an express therapeutic claim, the majority assumed that the intended-effects definition could be satisfied without one. It instead examined the entire statutory structure and Congress’s more specific tobacco enactments.

The majority reasoned that the Act required marketed drugs and devices to be safe and effective for intended use. On the FDA’s own findings, tobacco was dangerous as used, could not bear directions making its intended use safe, and could not satisfy the device-classification safety requirements. Jurisdiction under that scheme would therefore require removal from the market. Yet Congress’s tobacco laws contemplated continued commerce while informing consumers of tobacco’s hazards.

The FDA’s comparison between regulation and a harmful ban did not resolve that contradiction for the majority. The Act’s safety inquiry concerned therapeutic benefits outweighing risks to the consumer. Dangerous cancer therapies could satisfy that inquiry; the FDA had identified no comparable therapeutic benefit for tobacco. The majority did not say that every dangerous product must be banned.

sections.title: Congress’s tobacco legislation determines the result
paragraphs: The majority examined Congress’s affirmative tobacco legislation, its responses to other federal regulators, its restrictions on additional health-related labeling, and its repeated consideration of proposals expressly granting FDA authority. Those laws arose against the FDA’s longstanding disclaimers, subject to the therapeutic-claim exception. Together, they established a specific scheme reserving central tobacco-policy decisions to Congress.

The majority did not rely simply on failed bills or congressional silence, nor did it prohibit agencies from changing interpretations. The earlier agency position mattered because Congress had legislated against that understood allocation of authority. The breadth of the claimed power reinforced the conclusion: regulation of a major economic sector, potentially including a complete tobacco ban, was an extraordinary delegation to infer from general definitions and safety provisions.

Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas joined O’Connor. The Court affirmed the Fourth Circuit on March 21, 2000, concluding at Chevron’s first step that Congress had withheld the asserted authority. The seriousness of the public-health problem could not supply it. The Court left the alternative First Amendment challenge undecided.

sections.title: Four Justices would sustain jurisdiction
paragraphs: Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg, read the broad text, public-health purpose, and 1938 legislative history to encompass nontherapeutic products affecting bodily functions. Nicotine’s chemical action distinguished tobacco from ordinary objects such as clothing. Newly available industry documents supported objectively provable manufacturer intent without express therapeutic claims.

Breyer also rejected the premise that jurisdiction compelled a ban. Device provisions allowed remedial discretion and consideration of available alternatives; a regulated market could be safer than driving addicted consumers to dangerous substitutes. He disputed separating individual product risks from aggregate risks caused by the remedy.

The dissent found the later laws inconclusive: failed proposals pointed both ways, specific labeling restrictions did not foreclose other regulation, and the 1997 modernization law expressly preserved the jurisdictional question. Breyer understood prior disclaimers chiefly as reflecting insufficient evidence of manufacturer intent, a problem later evidence and scientific developments could overcome. Highly visible executive action could also promote political accountability. Those views did not carry the Court.
